# csv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/csv

## Expand description

The `csv` crate provides a fast and flexible CSV reader and writer, with
support for Serde.

The [tutorial](https://docs.rs/tutorial/index.html) is a good place to start if you’re new to
Rust.

The [cookbook](https://docs.rs/cookbook/index.html) will give you a variety of complete Rust
programs that do CSV reading and writing.

[§](https://docs.rs#brief-overview)Brief overview

**If you’re new to Rust**, you might find the
[tutorial](https://docs.rs/tutorial/index.html)
to be a good place to start.

The primary types in this crate are
[ Reader](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html)
and

[, for reading and writing CSV data respectively. Correspondingly, to support CSV data with custom field or record delimiters (among many other things), you should use either a](https://docs.rs/struct.Writer.html)

`Writer`[or a](https://docs.rs/struct.ReaderBuilder.html)

`ReaderBuilder`[, depending on whether you’re reading or writing CSV data.](https://docs.rs/struct.WriterBuilder.html)

`WriterBuilder`Unless you’re using Serde, the standard CSV record types are
[ StringRecord](https://docs.rs/struct.StringRecord.html)
and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteRecord.html)

`ByteRecord``StringRecord` should be used when you know your data to be valid UTF-8.
For data that may be invalid UTF-8, `ByteRecord` is suitable.Finally, the set of errors is described by the
[ Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
type.

The rest of the types in this crate mostly correspond to more detailed errors, position information, configuration knobs or iterator types.

[§](https://docs.rs#setup)Setup

Run `cargo add csv` to add the latest version of the `csv` crate to your
Cargo.toml.

If you want to use Serde’s custom derive functionality on your custom structs,
then run `cargo add serde --features derive` to add the `serde` crate with its
`derive` feature enabled to your `Cargo.toml`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example shows how to read CSV data from stdin and print each record to stdout.

There are more examples in the [cookbook](https://docs.rs/cookbook/index.html).

```
use std::{error::Error, io, process};
fn example() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    // Build the CSV reader and iterate over each record.
    let mut rdr = csv::Reader::from_reader(io::stdin());
    for result in rdr.records() {
        // The iterator yields Result<StringRecord, Error>, so we check the
        // error here.
        let record = result?;
        println!("{:?}", record);
    }
    Ok(())
}
fn main() {
    if let Err(err) = example() {
        println!("error running example: {}", err);
        process::exit(1);
    }
}
```
The above example can be run like so:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
$ git clone git://github.com/BurntSushi/rust-csv
$ cd rust-csv
$ cargo run --example cookbook-read-basic < examples/data/smallpop.csv
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-with-serde)Example with Serde

This example shows how to read CSV data from stdin into your own custom struct. By default, the member names of the struct are matched with the values in the header record of your CSV data.

```
use std::{error::Error, io, process};
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
struct Record {
    city: String,
    region: String,
    country: String,
    population: Option<u64>,
}
fn example() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut rdr = csv::Reader::from_reader(io::stdin());
    for result in rdr.deserialize() {
        // Notice that we need to provide a type hint for automatic
        // deserialization.
        let record: Record = result?;
        println!("{:?}", record);
    }
    Ok(())
}
fn main() {
    if let Err(err) = example() {
        println!("error running example: {}", err);
        process::exit(1);
    }
}
```
The above example can be run like so:

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- A cookbook of examples for CSV reading and writing.

- A tutorial for handling CSV data in Rust.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteRecord.html)- Record
- A single CSV record stored as raw bytes.
- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteRecordIter.html)- Record - Iter
- A double-ended iterator over the fields in a byte record.
- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteRecordsIntoIter.html)- Records - Into - Iter
- An owned iterator over records as raw bytes.
- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteRecordsIter.html)- Records - Iter
- A borrowed iterator over records as raw bytes.
- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/struct.DeserializeError.html)- Error
- An Serde deserialization error.
- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/struct.DeserializeRecordsIntoIter.html)- Records - Into - Iter
- An owned iterator over deserialized records.
- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/struct.DeserializeRecordsIter.html)- Records - Iter
- A borrowed iterator over deserialized records.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error that can occur when processing CSV data.
- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromUtf8Error.html)- Utf8 - Error
- A UTF-8 validation error during record conversion.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoInnerError.html)- Inner - Error
- `IntoInnerError`occurs when consuming a- `Writer`fails.
- [Position](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html)
- A position in CSV data.
- [Reader](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html)
- A already configured CSV reader.
- [Reader](https://docs.rs/struct.ReaderBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builds a CSV reader with various configuration knobs.
- [String](https://docs.rs/struct.StringRecord.html)- Record
- A single CSV record stored as valid UTF-8 bytes.
- [String](https://docs.rs/struct.StringRecordIter.html)- Record - Iter
- An iterator over the fields in a string record.
- [String](https://docs.rs/struct.StringRecordsIntoIter.html)- Records - Into - Iter
- An owned iterator over records as strings.
- [String](https://docs.rs/struct.StringRecordsIter.html)- Records - Iter
- A borrowed iterator over records as strings.
- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Error.html)- Error
- A UTF-8 validation error.
- [Writer](https://docs.rs/struct.Writer.html)
- An already configured CSV writer.
- [Writer](https://docs.rs/struct.WriterBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builds a CSV writer with various configuration knobs.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/enum.DeserializeErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind
- The type of a Serde deserialization error.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- The specific type of an error.
- [Quote](https://docs.rs/enum.QuoteStyle.html)- Style
- The quoting style to use when writing CSV data.
- [Terminator](https://docs.rs/enum.Terminator.html)
- A record terminator.
- [Trim](https://docs.rs/enum.Trim.html)
- The whitespace preservation behaviour when reading CSV data.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [invalid_](https://docs.rs/fn.invalid_option.html)- option
- A custom Serde deserializer for possibly invalid `Option<T>`fields.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A type alias for `Result<T, csv::Error>`.

# forward_to_deserialize_any in serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.226/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html

```
macro_rules! forward_to_deserialize_any {
    (<$visitor:ident: Visitor<$lifetime:tt>> $($func:ident)*) => { ... };
    ($($func:ident)*) => { ... };
}
```
**only.**

`docsrs`## Expand description

Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer` part of a new data format
for Serde.

Some [ Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html) implementations for self-describing formats do not
care what hint the

[gives them, they just want to blindly call the](https://docs.rs/de/trait.Visitor.html)

`Visitor`[method corresponding to the data they can tell is in the input. This requires repetitive implementations of all the](https://docs.rs/de/trait.Visitor.html)

`Visitor`[trait methods.](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)

`Deserializer`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[inline]
fn deserialize_bool<V>(self, visitor: V) -> Result<V::Value, Self::Error>
where
    V: Visitor<'de>,
{
    self.deserialize_any(visitor)
}
```
The `forward_to_deserialize_any!` macro implements these simple forwarding
methods so that they forward directly to [ Deserializer::deserialize_any](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html#tymethod.deserialize_any).
You can choose which methods to forward.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<'de> Deserializer<'de> for MyDeserializer {
    fn deserialize_any<V>(self, visitor: V) -> Result<V::Value, Self::Error>
    where
        V: Visitor<'de>,
    {
        /* ... */
    }
    forward_to_deserialize_any! {
        bool i8 i16 i32 i64 i128 u8 u16 u32 u64 u128 f32 f64 char str string
        bytes byte_buf option unit unit_struct newtype_struct seq tuple
        tuple_struct map struct enum identifier ignored_any
    }
}
```
The macro assumes the convention that your `Deserializer` lifetime parameter
is called `'de` and that the `Visitor` type parameters on each method are
called `V`. A different type parameter and a different lifetime can be
specified explicitly if necessary.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
forward_to_deserialize_any! {
    <W: Visitor<'q>>
    bool i8 i16 i32 i64 i128 u8 u16 u32 u64 u128 f32 f64 char str string
    bytes byte_buf option unit unit_struct newtype_struct seq tuple
    tuple_struct map struct enum identifier ignored_any
}
```

---

# Deserialize in serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.226/trait.Deserialize.html

`pub trait Deserialize<'de>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [deserialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.deserialize)<D>(deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, D::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)<'de>;
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be deserialized from any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Deserialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/de/index.html). All of these
can be deserialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called `serde_derive` to
automatically generate `Deserialize` implementations for structs and enums
in your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html) for how to
use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Deserialize` manually for
some type in your program. See the [Implementing
 Deserialize](https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html) section of the manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Deserialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the `linked-hash-map` crate provides a
`LinkedHashMap<K, V>` type that is deserializable by Serde because the crate
provides an implementation of `Deserialize` for it.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed by `Self` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Deserializing a data structure containing `Rc` will not attempt to
deduplicate `Rc` references to the same data. Every deserialized `Rc`
will end up with a strong count of 1.

[is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A **data format** that can deserialize any data structure supported by
Serde.

The role of this trait is to define the deserialization half of the [Serde
data model](https://serde.rs/data-model.html), which is a way to categorize every Rust data type into one of
29 possible types. Each method of the `Deserializer` trait corresponds to one
of the types of the data model.

Implementations of `Deserialize` map themselves into this data model by
passing to the `Deserializer` a `Visitor` implementation that can receive
these various types.

The types that make up the Serde data model are:

- **14 primitive types**- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
- f32, f64
- char

- **string**- UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
- When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing, there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.

- **byte array**- [u8]- Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be transient, owned, or borrowed.

- **option**- Either none or some value.

- **unit**- The type of `()`in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing no data.

- The type of
- **unit_struct**- For example `struct Unit`or`PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named value containing no data.

- For example
- **unit_variant**- For example the `E::A`and`E::B`in`enum E { A, B }`.

- For example the
- **newtype_struct**- For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

- For example
- **newtype_variant**- For example the `E::N`in`enum E { N(u8) }`.

- For example the
- **seq**- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example `Vec<T>`or`HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.

- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
- **tuple**- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `(u8,)`or`(String, u64, Vec<T>)`or`[u64; 10]`.

- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **tuple_struct**- A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.

- A named tuple, for example
- **tuple_variant**- For example the `E::T`in`enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.

- For example the
- **map**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example
- **struct**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized
data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized
data, for example
- **struct_variant**- For example the `E::S`in`enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.

- For example the

The `Deserializer` trait supports two entry point styles which enables
different kinds of deserialization.

-
The `deserialize_any`method. Self-describing data formats like JSON are able to look at the serialized data and tell what it represents. For example the JSON deserializer may see an opening curly brace (`{`) and know that it is seeing a map. If the data format supports`Deserializer::deserialize_any`, it will drive the Visitor using whatever type it sees in the input. JSON uses this approach when deserializing`serde_json::Value`which is an enum that can represent any JSON document. Without knowing what is in a JSON document, we can deserialize it to`serde_json::Value`by going through`Deserializer::deserialize_any`.
-
The various `deserialize_*`methods. Non-self-describing formats like Postcard need to be told what is in the input in order to deserialize it. The`deserialize_*`methods are hints to the deserializer for how to interpret the next piece of input. Non-self-describing formats are not able to deserialize something like`serde_json::Value`which relies on`Deserializer::deserialize_any`.

When implementing `Deserialize`, you should avoid relying on
`Deserializer::deserialize_any` unless you need to be told by the
Deserializer what type is in the input. Know that relying on
`Deserializer::deserialize_any` means your data type will be able to
deserialize from self-describing formats only, ruling out Postcard and many
others.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed from the input when deserializing. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-implementation)Example implementation

The [example data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html) presented on the website contains example code for
a basic JSON `Deserializer`.

instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/de/mod.rs.html#1253-1255)#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/de/mod.rs.html#1253-1255)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Deserialize` implementations should expect to
deserialize their human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::de::{self, Deserialize, Deserializer};
impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for Timestamp {
    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
    where
        D: Deserializer<'de>,
    {
        if deserializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Deserialize from a human-readable string like "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            let s = String::deserialize(deserializer)?;
            Timestamp::from_str(&s).map_err(de::Error::custom)
        } else {
            // Deserialize from a compact binary representation, seconds since
            // the Unix epoch.
            let n = u64::deserialize(deserializer)?;
            Ok(Timestamp::EPOCH + Duration::seconds(n))
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Serialize in serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.226/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Serializing a data structure containing `Rc` will serialize a copy of
the contents of the `Rc` each time the `Rc` is referenced within the
data structure. Serialization will not attempt to deduplicate these
repeated data.

}## Expand description

A **data format** that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

The role of this trait is to define the serialization half of the [Serde
data model](https://serde.rs/data-model.html), which is a way to categorize every Rust data structure into one
of 29 possible types. Each method of the `Serializer` trait corresponds to
one of the types of the data model.

Implementations of `Serialize` map themselves into this data model by
invoking exactly one of the `Serializer` methods.

The types that make up the Serde data model are:

- **14 primitive types**- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
- f32, f64
- char

- **string**- UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
- When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing, there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.

- **byte array**- [u8]- Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be transient, owned, or borrowed.

- **option**- Either none or some value.

- **unit**- The type of `()`in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing no data.

- The type of
- **unit_struct**- For example `struct Unit`or`PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named value containing no data.

- For example
- **unit_variant**- For example the `E::A`and`E::B`in`enum E { A, B }`.

- For example the
- **newtype_struct**- For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

- For example
- **newtype_variant**- For example the `E::N`in`enum E { N(u8) }`.

- For example the
- **seq**- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
`Vec<T>`or`HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.

- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
- **tuple**- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `(u8,)`or`(String, u64, Vec<T>)`or`[u64; 10]`.

- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **tuple_struct**- A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.

- A named tuple, for example
- **tuple_variant**- For example the `E::T`in`enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.

- For example the
- **map**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example
- **struct**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **struct_variant**- For example the `E::S`in`enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.

- For example the

Many Serde serializers produce text or binary data as output, for example
JSON or Postcard. This is not a requirement of the `Serializer` trait, and
there are serializers that do not produce text or binary output. One example
is the `serde_json::value::Serializer` (distinct from the main `serde_json`
serializer) that produces a `serde_json::Value` data structure in memory as
output.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-implementation)Example implementation

The [example data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html) presented on the website contains example code for
a basic JSON `Serializer`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

The output type produced by this `Serializer` during successful
serialization. Most serializers that produce text or binary output
should set `Ok = ()` and serialize into an [ io::Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) or buffer
contained within the

`Serializer` instance. Serializers that build
in-memory data structures may be simplified by using `Ok` to propagate
the data structure around.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize an `i8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i8` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i16` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i32` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize a `u8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u8` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u16` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u32` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize an `f32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `f32` and `f64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `f64` and
forward to `serialize_f64`.

Serialize a character.

If the format does not support characters, it is reasonable to serialize
it as a single element `str` or a `u32`.

Serialize a chunk of raw byte data.

Enables serializers to serialize byte slices more compactly or more
efficiently than other types of slices. If no efficient implementation
is available, a reasonable implementation would be to forward to
`serialize_seq`. If forwarded, the implementation looks usually just
like this:

Serialize a unit struct like `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`.

A reasonable implementation would be to forward to `serialize_unit`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Nothing;
impl Serialize for Nothing {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_unit_struct("Nothing")
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#889-894)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#889-894)

Serialize a unit variant like `E::A` in `enum E { A, B }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    A,
    B,
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::A => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 0, "A"),
            E::B => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 1, "B"),
        }
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

Serialize a newtype struct like `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

Serializers are encouraged to treat newtype structs as insignificant
wrappers around the data they contain. A reasonable implementation would
be to forward to `value.serialize(self)`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Millimeters(u8);
impl Serialize for Millimeters {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_newtype_struct("Millimeters", &self.0)
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#950-958)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#950-958)

Serialize a newtype variant like `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant. The `value` is the data contained within this newtype variant.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    M(String),
    N(u8),
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::M(ref s) => serializer.serialize_newtype_variant("E", 0, "M", s),
            E::N(n) => serializer.serialize_newtype_variant("E", 1, "N", &n),
        }
    }
}
```

    self,

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1006)

#### fn [serialize_seq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_seq)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeSeq](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeSeq), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a variably sized sequence. This call must be
followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`, then a call to
`end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the sequence, which may or may not be computable before the sequence is iterated. Some serializers only support sequences whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeSeq, Serializer};
impl<T> Serialize for Vec<T>
where
    T: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_seq(Some(self.len()))?;
        for element in self {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1062)#### fn [serialize_tuple](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_tuple)(
    self,
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeTuple](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeTuple), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1062)

#### fn [serialize_tuple](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_tuple)(
    self,
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeTuple](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeTuple), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a statically sized sequence whose length will be
known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized data.
This call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`,
then a call to `end`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
impl<A, B, C> Serialize for (A, B, C)
where
    A: Serialize,
    B: Serialize,
    C: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut tup = serializer.serialize_tuple(3)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.0)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.1)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.2)?;
        tup.end()
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
const VRAM_SIZE: usize = 386;
struct Vram([u16; VRAM_SIZE]);
impl Serialize for Vram {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_tuple(VRAM_SIZE)?;
        for element in &self.0[..] {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```

    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),

#### fn [serialize_tuple_struct](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_tuple_struct)(
    self,
    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),

Begin to serialize a tuple struct like `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`. This
call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_field`, then a
call to `end`.

The `name` is the name of the tuple struct and the `len` is the number
of data fields that will be serialized.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTupleStruct, Serializer};
struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);
impl Serialize for Rgb {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut ts = serializer.serialize_tuple_struct("Rgb", 3)?;
        ts.serialize_field(&self.0)?;
        ts.serialize_field(&self.1)?;
        ts.serialize_field(&self.2)?;
        ts.end()
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1134-1140)#### fn [serialize_tuple_variant](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_tuple_variant)(

    variant_index: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u32.html),
    variant: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeTupleVariant](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeTupleVariant), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

#### fn [serialize_tuple_variant](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_tuple_variant)(
    self,
    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    variant_index: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u32.html),
    variant: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeTupleVariant](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeTupleVariant), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a tuple variant like `E::T` in `enum E { T(u8, u8) }`. This call must be followed by zero or more calls to
`serialize_field`, then a call to `end`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, the `variant` is the name of the variant,
and the `len` is the number of data fields that will be serialized.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTupleVariant, Serializer};
enum E {
    T(u8, u8),
    U(String, u32, u32),
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::T(ref a, ref b) => {
                let mut tv = serializer.serialize_tuple_variant("E", 0, "T", 2)?;
                tv.serialize_field(a)?;
                tv.serialize_field(b)?;
                tv.end()
            }
            E::U(ref a, ref b, ref c) => {
                let mut tv = serializer.serialize_tuple_variant("E", 1, "U", 3)?;
                tv.serialize_field(a)?;
                tv.serialize_field(b)?;
                tv.serialize_field(c)?;
                tv.end()
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1188)#### fn [serialize_map](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_map)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeMap](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeMap), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1188)

#### fn [serialize_map](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_map)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeMap](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeMap), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a map. This call must be followed by zero or more
calls to `serialize_key` and `serialize_value`, then a call to `end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the map, which may or may not be computable before the map is iterated. Some serializers only support maps whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeMap, Serializer};
impl<K, V> Serialize for HashMap<K, V>
where
    K: Serialize,
    V: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut map = serializer.serialize_map(Some(self.len()))?;
        for (k, v) in self {
            map.serialize_entry(k, v)?;
        }
        map.end()
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1220-1224)#### fn [serialize_struct](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_struct)(
    self,
    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeStruct](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeStruct), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1220-1224)

#### fn [serialize_struct](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_struct)(
    self,
    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeStruct](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeStruct), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a struct like `struct Rgb { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.
This call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_field`,
then a call to `end`.

The `name` is the name of the struct and the `len` is the number of
data fields that will be serialized. `len` does not include fields
which are skipped with [ SerializeStruct::skip_field](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.SerializeStruct.html#method.skip_field).

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Rgb {
    r: u8,
    g: u8,
    b: u8,
}
impl Serialize for Rgb {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut rgb = serializer.serialize_struct("Rgb", 3)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("r", &self.r)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("g", &self.g)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("b", &self.b)?;
        rgb.end()
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1264-1270)#### fn [serialize_struct_variant](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_struct_variant)(
    self,
    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    variant_index: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u32.html),
    variant: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeStructVariant](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeStructVariant), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1264-1270)

#### fn [serialize_struct_variant](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_struct_variant)(
    self,
    name: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    variant_index: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u32.html),
    variant: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeStructVariant](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeStructVariant), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a struct variant like `E::S` in `enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`. This call must be followed by zero or more calls to
`serialize_field`, then a call to `end`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, the `variant` is the name of the variant,
and the `len` is the number of data fields that will be serialized.
`len` does not include fields which are skipped with
[ SerializeStructVariant::skip_field](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.SerializeStructVariant.html#method.skip_field).

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStructVariant, Serializer};
enum E {
    S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 },
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::S {
                ref r,
                ref g,
                ref b,
            } => {
                let mut sv = serializer.serialize_struct_variant("E", 0, "S", 3)?;
                sv.serialize_field("r", r)?;
                sv.serialize_field("g", g)?;
                sv.serialize_field("b", b)?;
                sv.end()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

impl Serialize for i128 {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_i128(*self)
    }
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1296-1305)

#### fn [collect_seq](https://docs.rs#method.collect_seq)<I>(self, iter: I) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Collect an iterator as a sequence.

The default implementation serializes each item yielded by the iterator
using [ serialize_seq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_seq). Implementors should not need to override this
method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct SecretlyOneHigher {
    data: Vec<i32>,
}
impl Serialize for SecretlyOneHigher {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_seq(self.data.iter().map(|x| x + 1))
    }
}
```

#### fn [collect_map](https://docs.rs#method.collect_map)<K, V, I>(self, iter: I) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Collect an iterator as a map.

The default implementation serializes each pair yielded by the iterator
using [ serialize_map](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_map). Implementors should not need to override this
method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
use std::collections::BTreeSet;
struct MapToUnit {
    keys: BTreeSet<i32>,
}
// Serializes as a map in which the values are all unit.
impl Serialize for MapToUnit {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_map(self.keys.iter().map(|k| (k, ())))
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1373-1378)#### fn [collect_str](https://docs.rs#method.collect_str)<T>(self, value: [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

#### fn [collect_str](https://docs.rs#method.collect_str)<T>(self, value: [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

**crate features**only.

`std` or `alloc`Serialize a string produced by an implementation of `Display`.

The default implementation builds a heap-allocated [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/string/struct.String.html) and
delegates to

[. Serializers are encouraged to provide a more efficient implementation if possible.](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#tymethod.serialize_str)

`serialize_str`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for DateTime {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_str(&format_args!("{:?}{:?}", self.naive_local(), self.offset()))
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Serialize` implementations should serialize in
human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for Timestamp {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        if serializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Serialize to a human-readable string "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            self.to_string().serialize(serializer)
        } else {
            // Serialize to a compact binary representation.
            self.seconds_since_epoch().serialize(serializer)
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)```
use serde::ser::Serialize;
use serde_derive::Serialize;
use std::fmt::{self, Display};
#[derive(Serialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "kebab-case")]
pub enum MessageType {
    StartRequest,
    EndRequest,
}
impl Display for MessageType {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        self.serialize(f)
    }
}
```

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0.74/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

---

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0.35/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2.0.81/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Abi](https://docs.rs/struct.Abi.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The binary interface of a function: `extern "C"`.
- [Angle](https://docs.rs/struct.AngleBracketedGenericArguments.html)- Bracketed - Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed arguments of a path segment: the `<K, V>`in`HashMap<K, V>`.
- [Arm](https://docs.rs/struct.Arm.html)- `full`
- One arm of a `match`expression:`0..=10 => { return true; }`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocConst.html)- Const - `derive`or- `full`
- An equality constraint on an associated constant: the `PANIC = false`in`Trait<PANIC = false>`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A binding (equality constraint) on an associated type: the `Item = u8`in`Iterator<Item = u8>`.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.Attribute.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An attribute, like `#[repr(transparent)]`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareFnArg.html)- FnArg - `derive`or- `full`
- An argument in a function type: the `usize`in`fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareVariadic.html)- Variadic - `derive`or- `full`
- The variadic argument of a function pointer like `fn(usize, ...)`.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)- `full`
- A braced block containing Rust statements.
- [Bound](https://docs.rs/struct.BoundLifetimes.html)- Lifetimes - `derive`or- `full`
- A set of bound lifetimes: `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A const generic parameter: `const LENGTH: usize`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.Constraint.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An associated type bound: `Iterator<Item: Display>`.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataEnum.html)- Enum - `derive`
- An enum input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`
- A struct input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataUnion.html)- Union - `derive`
- An untagged union input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Derive](https://docs.rs/struct.DeriveInput.html)- Input - `derive`
- Data structure sent to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error returned when a Syn parser cannot parse the input tokens.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprArray.html)- Array - `full`
- A slice literal expression: `[a, b, c, d]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAssign.html)- Assign - `full`
- An assignment expression: `a = compute()`.

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAwait.html)- Await - `full`
- An await expression: `fut.await`.

- A binary operation: `a + b`,`a += b`.

- A blocked scope: `{ ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBreak.html)- Break - `full`
- A `break`, with an optional label to break and an optional expression.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCall.html)- Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A function call expression: `invoke(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCast.html)- Cast - `derive`or- `full`

- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprContinue.html)- Continue - `full`
- A `continue`, with an optional label.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprField.html)- Field - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprForLoop.html)- ForLoop - `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprGroup.html)- Group - `full`
- An expression contained within invisible delimiters.
- [ExprIf](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIf.html)- `full`
- An `if`expression with an optional`else`block:`if expr { ... } else { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIndex.html)- Index - `derive`or- `full`
- A square bracketed indexing expression: `vector[2]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprInfer.html)- Infer - `full`
- The inferred value of a const generic argument, denoted `_`.
- [ExprLet](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLet.html)- `full`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attr](https://docs.rs/enum.AttrStyle.html)- Style - `derive`or- `full`
- Distinguishes between attributes that decorate an item and attributes that are contained within an item.
- [BinOp](https://docs.rs/enum.BinOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operator: `+`,`+=`,`&`.
- [Captured](https://docs.rs/enum.CapturedParam.html)- Param - `full`
- Single parameter in a precise capturing bound.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/enum.Data.html)- `derive`
- The storage of a struct, enum or union data structure.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A Rust expression.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldMutability.html)- Mutability - `derive`or- `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Fields](https://docs.rs/enum.Fields.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Data stored within an enum variant or struct.
- [FnArg](https://docs.rs/enum.FnArg.html)- `full`
- An argument in a function signature: the `n: usize`in`fn f(n: usize)`.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/enum.ForeignItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an `extern`block.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericArgument.html)- Argument - `derive`or- `full`
- An individual generic argument, like `'a`,`T`, or`Item = T`.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A generic type parameter, lifetime, or const generic: `T: Into<String>`,`'a: 'b`,`const LEN: usize`.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplRestriction.html)- Restriction - `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/enum.Item.html)- `full`
- Things that can appear directly inside of a module or scope.
- [Lit](https://docs.rs/enum.Lit.html)
- A Rust literal such as a string or integer or boolean.
- [Macro](https://docs.rs/enum.MacroDelimiter.html)- Delimiter - `derive`or- `full`
- A grouping token that surrounds a macro body: `m!(...)`or`m!{...}`or`m![...]`.
- [Member](https://docs.rs/enum.Member.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A struct or tuple struct field accessed in a struct literal or field expression.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/enum.Meta.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Content of a compile-time structured attribute.
- [Pat](https://docs.rs/enum.Pat.html)- `full`
- A pattern in a local binding, function signature, match expression, or various other places.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/enum.PathArguments.html)- Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed or parenthesized arguments of a path segment.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/enum.PointerMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- Mutability of a raw pointer (`*const T`,`*mut T`), in which non-mutable isn’t the implicit default.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/enum.RangeLimits.html)- Limits - `full`
- Limit types of a range, inclusive or exclusive.
- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- Return type of a function signature.
- [Static](https://docs.rs/enum.StaticMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- The mutability of an `Item::Static`or`ForeignItem::Static`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)- `full`
- A statement, usually ending in a semicolon.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitBoundModifier.html)- Bound - Modifier - `derive`or- `full`
- A modifier on a trait bound, currently only used for the `?`in`?Sized`.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item declaration within the definition of a trait.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The possible types that a Rust value could have.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeParamBound.html)- Param - Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait or lifetime used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [UnOp](https://docs.rs/enum.UnOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A unary operator: `*`,`!`,`-`.
- [UseTree](https://docs.rs/enum.UseTree.html)- `full`
- A suffix of an import tree in a `use`item:`Type as Renamed`or`*`.
- [Visibility](https://docs.rs/enum.Visibility.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The visibility level of an item: inherited or `pub`or`pub(restricted)`.
- [Where](https://docs.rs/enum.WherePredicate.html)- Predicate - `derive`or- `full`
- A single predicate in a `where`clause:`T: Deserialize<'de>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)- `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse tokens of source code into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse2](https://docs.rs/fn.parse2.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a proc-macro2 token stream into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_file.html)- file - `full`and- `parsing`
- Parse the content of a file of Rust code.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_str.html)- str - `parsing`
- Parse a string of Rust code into the chosen syntax tree node.
